title: Leading When The Machines Get Loud
author: Andrea Chiarelli
source: Andrea Chiarelli and Diamantino Almeida (andreachiarelli.substack.com), October 30, 2025
summary: The piece argues that leaders who treat AI as a universal solution risk becoming operators of tools rather than leaders of people. It names the Operator's Trap, where leaders burn hours tuning prompts and mistake that for leadership, and shows how reflexive consultation of AI erodes trust and feedback loops within teams. It then traces the social cost: meetings become summaries, conversations become transcripts, and shared endeavor fades. The remedy is deliberate design in which AI is an analytical partner and humans keep judgment, meaning-making and productive disagreement. The case is made for Leadership because its subject is how a leader's relationship to AI at work shapes trust, culture and team dynamics.
points: Spending hours refining prompts can become micromanagement disguised as innovation, because a model offers no growth to nurture and responds to parameters, not purpose.
Turning to AI for validation moves confidence from colleagues to tools, collapsing the human feedback loops that sustain trust.
Automating meetings and conversations converts collaboration into coordination and erodes the shared endeavor that sustains purpose.
Technology can simulate reasoning but cannot assign meaning, so deciding what should be done remains a human responsibility.
Leaders should bring teams together to test what AI surfaces and keep the productive friction that sparks progress.
quotes: Leadership has always been forged through experience: through criticism, setbacks, learning, and growth. No algorithm can replicate the insight that comes from navigating uncertainty with others.
When an AI model performs well, there is no growth to celebrate; when it fails, there is no learning process to nurture. Machines respond to parameters, not purpose.

As teams grow accustomed to consulting AI for validation (“Let me check that with ChatGPT”) trust within human networks begins to erode. Confidence moves from colleagues to tools, and with that shift, feedback loops collapse. People stop seeking affirmation from each other, and start seeking it from the interface.

Meetings become summaries, conversations become transcripts, and teamwork becomes coordination rather than collaboration. What is lost is not efficiency, but the sense of shared endeavor that sustains purpose.

Technology can simulate reasoning, but it cannot assign meaning. The ability to discern significance, to decide what should be done, not merely what can be done, remains an exclusively human responsibility.

True leadership cultivates environments where people feel safe to experiment and disagree productively. It values the human friction that sparks progress, rather than seeking to eliminate it through automation.
